questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | GA Q3
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question: An electricity utility company charges ₹ 7 per kWh (kilo watt-hour). If a 40-watt desk light is left on for 10 hours each night for 180 days, what would be the cost of energy consumption? If the desk light is on for 2 more hours each night for the 180 days, what would be the percentage-increase in the cost of energy consumption?
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Numerical Computation and Estimation

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Core Concept(s): Energy calculation, Percentage increase.
  • Given: Power \(P = 40\text{ W}\), Initial Time \(t_1 = 10\text{ hours/day}\) for \(180\text{ days}\), Rate \(= 7\text{ INR per kWh}\). Additional time \(\Delta t = 2\text{ hours/day}\).
  • Find: Total baseline cost and percentage increase in cost.

Solution

  • Governing Formulas:
    \[\text{Energy (kWh)} = \dfrac{P \times t_{\text{total}}}{1000}\]\[\text{Cost} = \text{Energy} \times \text{Rate}\]\[\text{\% Increase} = \left(\dfrac{\Delta t}{t_1}\right) \times 100\]
  • Step 1: Calculate initial energy consumption: \[E_1 = \dfrac{40 \times 10 \times 180}{1000} = 72\text{ kWh}\]
  • Step 2: Calculate base cost: \[\text{Cost} = 72 \times 7 = 504\text{ INR}\]
  • Step 3: Calculate percentage increase. Since the power rate is constant, the percentage increase in energy cost is directly proportional to the percentage increase in daily operating time: \[\text{\% Increase} = \dfrac{2}{10} \times 100 = 20\%\]

Final Answer

Answer: Option (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | GA Q5
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question:
A bag contains Violet (V), Yellow (Y), Red (R), and Green (G) balls. On counting them, the following results are obtained:
(i) The sum of Yellow balls and twice the number of Violet balls is 50.
(ii) The sum of Violet and Green balls is 50.
(iii) The sum of Yellow and Red balls is 50.
(iv) The sum of Violet and twice the number of Red balls is 50.
Which one of the following Pie charts correctly represents the balls in the bag?
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Numerical Computation and Estimation

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Core Concept(s): Simultaneous linear equations, Pie chart percentages.
  • Given: Four unknown variables (V, Y, R, G) mapped to equations:
    \(Y + 2V = 50\)
    \(V + G = 50\)
    \(Y + R = 50\)
    \(V + 2R = 50\)
  • Find: The correct pie chart distribution for the colors.

Solution

  • Governing Logic: Solve the linear system for absolute quantities, sum them up, and convert to constituent percentages.
  • Step 1: From equation (4), express R: \(2R = 50 - V \implies R = 25 - 0.5V\)
  • Step 2: From equation (1), express Y: \(Y = 50 - 2V\)
  • Step 3: Substitute \(Y\) and \(R\) into equation (3): \[(50 - 2V) + (25 - 0.5V) = 50\] \[75 - 2.5V = 50 \implies 2.5V = 25 \implies V = 10\]
  • Step 4: Substitute \(V = 10\) back into the expressions:
    \(Y = 50 - 2(10) = 30\)
    \(G = 50 - 10 = 40\) (from eq. 2)
    \(R = 25 - 0.5(10) = 20\)
  • Step 5: Total balls \(= V + Y + R + G = 10 + 30 + 20 + 40 = 100\).
    Percentages directly equal the absolute counts: V = 10%, Y = 30%, R = 20%, G = 40%.

Final Answer

Answer: Option (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | GA Q8
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question:
Consider a five-digit number \( PQRST \) that has distinct digits \( P, Q, R, S, \) and \( T \), and satisfies the following conditions:
\[P < Q \]
\[S > P > T \]
\[R < T \]
If integers 1 through 5 are used to construct such a number, the value of \( P \) is:
questions.explanation:
Analytical Aptitude → Numerical Relations and Reasoning

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Core Concept(s): Inequalities and distinct integer assignment.
  • Given: A 5-digit number PQRST with distinct digits from the set \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}\).
    Constraints: \(P < Q\), \(S > P > T\), and \(R < T\).
  • Find: The required integer value of digit \(P\).

Solution

  • Rule/Logic: Chain the inequalities to fix relative hierarchies, then assign elements from the tightly bounded constraint set.
  • Step 1: Combine \(S > P > T\) and \(R < T\) into a strict descending chain: \(S > P > T > R\).
  • Step 2: Because the digits must be distinct positive integers, \(R\) and \(T\) consume the smallest possible available numbers. At a minimum, \(R \ge 1\) and \(T \ge 2\). Thus, \(P\) must be at least \(3\).
  • Step 3: We also have the condition \(P < Q\). This means \(Q\) must be strictly greater than \(P\).
  • Step 4: Test \(P = 4\): If \(P = 4\), then \(S\) must be 5 (since \(S > P\)). But \(Q\) must also be \(> P\), meaning \(Q\) would also have to be 5. This violates the "distinct digits" rule.
  • Step 5: Therefore, \(P\) can only be 3. (Assigning \(R=1, T=2\), leaving \(\{4, 5\}\) exclusively for \(S\) and \(Q\).)

Final Answer

Answer: Option (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | GA Q9
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question:
A business person buys potatoes of two different varieties P and Q, mixes them in a certain ratio and sells them at ₹ 192 per kg.
The cost of the variety P is ₹ 800 for 5 kg.
The cost of the variety Q is ₹ 800 for 4 kg.
If the person gets 8% profit, what is the P:Q ratio (by weight)?
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Numerical Computation and Estimation

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Core Concept(s): Cost price, selling price, profit percentage, and mixtures (Alligation).
  • Given:
    • Selling Price (SP) of mixture = ₹192/kg
    • Required Profit = 8%
    • Cost of P = ₹800 for 5 kg
    • Cost of Q = ₹800 for 4 kg
  • Find: The mixing ratio of P:Q by weight.

Solution

  • Governing Formulas:
    \[\text{Cost Price (CP)} = \dfrac{\text{SP}}{1 + (\text{Profit \%} / 100)}\]\[\text{Alligation Ratio} = \dfrac{CP_Q - CP_{mix}}{CP_{mix} - CP_P}\]
  • Step 1: Determine Cost Price of the finalized mixture: \[CP_{mix} = \dfrac{192}{1.08} = \dfrac{19200}{108} = \dfrac{1600}{9} \text{ INR/kg}\]
  • Step 2: Determine individual raw Cost Prices: \[CP_P = \dfrac{800}{5} = 160 \text{ INR/kg}\] \[CP_Q = \dfrac{800}{4} = 200 \text{ INR/kg}\]
  • Step 3: Apply the rule of Alligation: \[\text{Ratio } (P:Q) = \dfrac{200 - \dfrac{1600}{9}}{\dfrac{1600}{9} - 160} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1800 - 1600}{9}}{\dfrac{1600 - 1440}{9}} = \dfrac{200}{160} = \dfrac{5}{4}\]

Final Answer

Answer: Option (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | GA Q10
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question:
Three villages P, Q, and R are located in such a way that the distance PQ = 13 km, QR = 14 km, and RP = 15 km, as shown in the figure. A straight road joins Q and R. It is proposed to connect P to this road QR by constructing another road. What is the minimum possible length (in km) of this connecting road?
Note: The figure shown is representative.
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Mensuration and Geometry

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Core Concept(s): Properties of triangles, minimum distance (altitude).
  • Given: A triangle PQR with side lengths \(PQ = 13\text{ km}\), \(QR = 14\text{ km}\), and \(RP = 15\text{ km}\).
  • Find: Minimum possible length of a connecting road from vertex P to line QR.

Solution

  • Rule/Logic: The shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular altitude. Calculate the triangle's area using Heron's formula, then back-calculate the height.
  • Step 1: Calculate the semi-perimeter \((s)\): \[s = \dfrac{13 + 14 + 15}{2} = 21\text{ km}\]
  • Step 2: Calculate Area \((A)\) using Heron's formula: \[A = \sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)} = \sqrt{21(21-14)(21-15)(21-13)}\] \[A = \sqrt{21 \times 7 \times 6 \times 8} = \sqrt{7056} = 84\text{ km}^2\]
  • Step 3: Calculate the perpendicular altitude \((h)\) to base \(QR = 14\): \[A = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times h \implies 84 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 14 \times h\] \[84 = 7h \implies h = 12\text{ km}\]

Final Answer

Answer: Option (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q11
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
For the matrix \([A]\) given below, the transpose is _______.
\[[A] = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 1 & 4 & 5 \\ 4 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\]
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Matrix Algebra (Transpose)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given Data: 3×3 square matrix [A] with elements: Row 1 = [2, 3, 4], Row 2 = [1, 4, 5], Row 3 = [4, 3, 2].
  • Aim: Identify the transpose matrix from the four options.

Core Concepts:

Transpose operation: \([A]^T = [A_{ji}]\) where every element \(a_{ij}\) of the original becomes \(a_{ji}\). Rows of \([A]\) become columns of \([A]^T\) (and vice-versa). Property: \(([A]^T)^T = [A]\).

Common pitfalls: Mixing with adjoint (cofactors) or inverse.

Solution:

  1. Column 1 of [A] → Row 1 of \([A]^T\) → [2, 1, 4]
  2. Column 2 of [A] → Row 2 of \([A]^T\) → [3, 4, 3]
  3. Column 3 of [A] → Row 3 of \([A]^T\) → [4, 5, 2]
  4. Resulting transpose matrix:
    \[[A]^T = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 4 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\]
  5. Exact match with option (A).

Final Answer:

\(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 4 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) | Option(s): A

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q12
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
Integration of \( ln(x) \) with x i.e.,
\( \displaystyle \int ln(x) dx = \) ______.
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Integral Calculus (Indefinite Integration)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Application
  • Given Data: Integrand \(= \ln(x)\) (natural logarithm, \(x > 0\)).
  • Aim: Evaluate indefinite integral \(\int \ln(x)\, dx\) and match with the correct option.

Core Concepts:

Integration by Parts Formula: \(\int u\, dv = uv - \int v\, du\)

Choose \(u = \ln(x)\) (easy to differentiate) and \(dv = dx\) (easy to integrate).

Common pitfalls: Forgetting the \(-x\) term or sign error in parts.

Solution:

  1. Let \(u = \ln(x) \Rightarrow du = \dfrac{1}{x}\, dx\)
  2. \(dv = dx \Rightarrow v = x\)
  3. Apply integration by parts:
    \[\int \ln(x)\, dx = x\ln(x) - \int x \cdot \dfrac{1}{x}\, dx\]
  4. Simplify the remaining integral:
    \[= x\ln(x) - \int 1\, dx = x\ln(x) - x + C\]
  5. Verification by differentiation:
    \[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[x\ln(x) - x\right] = \ln(x) + x \cdot \dfrac{1}{x} - 1 = \ln(x) \quad \checkmark\]

Final Answer:

\(x\ln(x) - x + C\) | Option(s): A

questions.question:
Consider the following statements (P) and (Q):
(P): Fly ash and ground granulated blast furnace slag can be used as mineral admixtures in concrete.
(Q): As per IS 456:2000, the minimum moist curing period becomes higher when a mineral admixture is added to concrete.
Identify the CORRECT option from choices given below.
questions.explanation:
Concrete Technology | Mineral Admixtures & Curing (IS 456:2000)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Recall
  • Given Data: Two statements (P) and (Q) to be evaluated.
  • Aim: Determine truth values of both statements and select the correct combination.

Core Concepts:

Mineral admixtures = supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs): Fly ash (IS 3812 Part 1/2), GGBS (IS 12089).

IS 456:2000 Clause 5.2.1–5.2.2 & Clause 13.5.1–13.5.2 (Moist Curing): OPC requires a minimum of 7 days moist curing. The pozzolanic reaction of fly ash/GGBS is slower, so the minimum moist curing period increases to 10 days (or more in hot/dry weather) to ensure adequate strength gain and durability.

Common pitfalls: Assuming curing period remains 7 days for all mix types.

Solution:

  1. Statement (P): Fly ash and GGBS are explicitly listed as mineral admixtures permitted in concrete (IS 456 Table 5, Clause 5.2) → TRUE.
  2. Statement (Q): Because of slower pozzolanic hydration, IS 456:2000 stipulates a higher minimum moist curing duration (≥10 days) when mineral admixtures replace part of cement → TRUE.

Both (P) and (Q) are TRUE | Option(s): A

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q14
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
Consider the pin-jointed truss shown in the figure. Influence line is drawn for the axial force in the member G-I, when a unit load travels on the bottom chord of the truss. Identify the CORRECT influence line from the following options:
Note: Positive value corresponds to tension and negative value corresponds to compression in the member.
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Influence Lines for Trusses (Moving Load)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data: Pin-jointed truss, 6 panels × 6 m = 36 m span, bottom chord joints A–D–G–I–L–O–P, height = 3 m (parallel-chord configuration), unit vertical load travels along bottom chord. Member = G–I (bottom chord panel). Positive = tension, negative = compression.
  • Aim: Identify the correct shape and peak location of the influence line for axial force in member G–I.

Core Concepts:

For a parallel-chord truss, the bottom-chord force is approximated as:

\[F_{G\text{-}I} = \dfrac{M_{\text{section}}}{h}\]

where \(M_{\text{section}}\) is the bending moment at the panel section from a free-body diagram and \(h\) = vertical distance between chords (= 3 m).

The Influence Line Diagram (ILD) is piecewise linear, changing slope only at panel points. The bottom chord remains in tension for a downward unit load, so all ordinates are positive.

Common pitfalls: Wrong section cut, sign error, or peak placed at wrong joint.

Solution:

  1. Locate G–I panel: G at 12 m, I at 18 m from A (central panel).
  2. For unit load left of G (e.g., at A or D): left reaction \(R_A = (36 - s)/36\); moment about the appropriate top joint gives a positive (tension) force in G–I rising linearly.
  3. At load exactly at G: maximum ordinate reaches \(+1.33\) (from the 6 m panel and 3 m height lever arm geometry, yielding a factor of \(4/3\)).
  4. For unit load right of G (I to P): force decreases linearly to zero at P (right reaction dominates).
  5. Overall shape: linear increase from A (0) to peak \(+1.33\) exactly at G, then linear decrease to P (0); no sign reversal (bottom chord always in tension).
  6. This matches option (B) exactly; options (A) & (C) place the peak at wrong joints (D or I), and option (D) shows an erroneous compression segment.

Final Answer:

ILD peaking at \(+1.33\) at G then linearly decreasing to P (all positive, tension throughout) | Option(s): B

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q15
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: The most suitable test for measuring the permeability of clayey soils in the laboratory is _______.
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Soil Permeability (Laboratory Testing)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given Data: Clayey soil (low permeability, \(k\) typically \(< 10^{-7}~m/s\)).
  • Aim: Select the most suitable laboratory permeability test.

Core Concepts:

Darcy's Law: \(v = k\,i\), where \(v\) = discharge velocity, \(k\) = coefficient of permeability, \(i\) = hydraulic gradient.

  • Constant-head test (IS 2720 Part 17): Suitable for coarse-grained soils (\(k > 10^{-5}~m/s\)) — maintains steady head with measurable discharge.
  • Falling-head test (IS 2720 Part 17): Suitable for fine-grained soils (\(k < 10^{-5}~m/s\)) — measures time for head drop in standpipe, ideal for clays where discharge is too small for constant-head accuracy.
  • Pumping-out test: Field test only.
  • Hydrometer test: Used for particle size analysis (IS 2720 Part 4), not permeability.

Standard assumption: Laminar flow (Re < 1).

Solution:

  1. Clayey soils have very low \(k\) → constant-head test gives negligible measurable outflow.
  2. Falling-head test allows measurement of time for head drop in standpipe using the formula:
    \[k = \dfrac{2.303\, a\, L}{A\, t} \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{h_1}{h_2}\right)\]where \(a\) = standpipe area, \(L\) = sample length, \(A\) = sample cross-sectional area, \(t\) = elapsed time.
  3. Hence, most suitable test = Falling head test.

Final Answer:

Falling head test | Option(s): D

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q16
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A hydraulic jump occurs in an open channel when the slope of the channel changes from _______.
options: STEEP slope to a STEEPER slope

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: STEEP slope to a STEEPER slope
structuredOptions.html: STEEP slope to a STEEPER slope

questions.explanation:
Hydraulics & Hydraulic Machines | Open Channel Flow (Hydraulic Jump)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Application
  • Given Data: Open channel with a change in bed slope.
  • Aim: Identify the condition for occurrence of a hydraulic jump.

Core Concepts:

Froude number: \(Fr = \dfrac{v}{\sqrt{g\,y}}\)

  • Supercritical flow: \(Fr > 1\) (steep slope, \(S_0 > S_c\))
  • Subcritical flow: \(Fr < 1\) (mild slope, \(S_0 < S_c\))

A hydraulic jump occurs when flow transitions from supercritical to subcritical, dissipating energy at the slope break. The reverse transition (mild to steep) produces no jump — flow simply accelerates smoothly.

Solution:

  1. Steep slope → uniform supercritical flow (\(Fr > 1\)).
  2. Sudden change to mild slope → normal depth becomes subcritical → a hydraulic jump forms to match the downstream depth condition.
  3. Transition from mild to steep causes no jump (flow accelerates).
  4. Hence, hydraulic jump occurs at: Steep slope → Mild slope.

Final Answer:

STEEP slope to MILD slope | Option(s): B

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q17
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: The bacteria mainly responsible for crown corrosion in a sewer is _______.
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Engineering (Sewer Corrosion)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data: Crown region of a sewer pipe (aerobic zone).
  • Aim: Identify the bacteria responsible for crown corrosion.

Core Concepts:

The biochemical pathway of crown corrosion proceeds in two stages:

  • Anaerobic zone (sewer bottom): Sulphate Reducing Bacteria (SRB), e.g., Desulfovibrio, reduce \(SO_4^{2-}\) to \(H_2S\) gas.
  • Aerobic zone (crown): \(H_2S\) rises to the crown and is oxidised by aerobic sulphur-oxidising bacteria (Thiobacillus thiooxidans) to \(H_2SO_4\) (pH drops to <2) → concrete corrosion.

Other bacteria are unrelated: Methanogenic (methane production), Denitrifying (\(NO_3^-\) reduction), Pseudomonas (general heterotroph).

Solution:

  1. SRB produce \(H_2S\) anaerobically at the sewer bottom.
  2. \(H_2S\) gas diffuses upward to the crown.
  3. Aerobic oxidation of \(H_2S\) → \(H_2SO_4\) → crown corrosion.
  4. The primarily responsible group initiating the process = Sulphur reducing bacteria.

  • Aim: Identify correct expressions for the z-component of curl and divergence.

Core Concepts:

Curl in Cartesian coordinates:

\[\nabla \times \vec{V} = \left(\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial z}\right)\hat{x} + \left(\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z} - \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x}\right)\hat{y} + \left(\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)\hat{z}\]

For 2-D flow (\(w=0\), \(\partial/\partial z = 0\)), the z-component simplifies to \(\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}\).

Divergence (continuity for incompressible flow):

\[\nabla \cdot \vec{V} = \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y} + \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial z}\]

Reduces to \(\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y}\) for 2-D flow.

Common pitfall: Confusing the sign in curl (remember the right-hand rule).

  1. z-component of curl: Substitute \(w=0\) → \(\left(\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)\hat{z}\) → matches option (A). Option (B) has reversed sign → incorrect.
  2. Divergence: \(\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y}\) → matches option (C). Option (D) uses cross derivatives → incorrect.

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: \(b = 250~mm\), \(d = 500~mm\), design shear strength \(\tau_c = 0.3~N/mm^2\), pure torsion (\(V_u = 0\)).
  • Aim: Find the torsional moment capacity \(T_u\) in kN·m, rounded to 1 decimal place.

Core Concepts:

As per IS 456:2000 Cl. 41.4.3, the equivalent shear is:

\[V_e = V_u + 1.6\,\dfrac{T_u}{b}\]

For pure torsion (\(V_u = 0\)), the equivalent shear stress becomes:

\[\tau_{ve} = \dfrac{1.6\,T_u}{b^2\,d} \leq \tau_c\]

Rearranging for torsional capacity:

\[T_u = \dfrac{\tau_c \times b^2 \times d}{1.6}\]

Solution:

  1. \(b^2 = 250 \times 250 = 62{,}500~mm^2\)
  2. \(b^2 \times d = 62{,}500 \times 500 = 31{,}250{,}000~mm^3\)
  3. \(\tau_c \times b^2 \times d = 0.3 \times 31{,}250{,}000 = 9{,}375{,}000~N\cdot mm\)
  4. \(T_u = \dfrac{9{,}375{,}000}{1.6} = 5{,}859{,}375~N\cdot mm = 5.859~kN\cdot m\)
  5. Rounded to one decimal place: 5.9 kN·m.

Final Answer:

5.9 kN·m | Option(s): 5.7 to 6.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q31
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
From a flow-net diagram drawn under a concrete dam, following information are obtained: (i) The head difference between upstream and downstream side of the dam is 9 m. (ii) The total number of equipotential drops between upstream and downstream side of the dam is 10. (iii) The length of the field nearest to the toe of the dam in the downstream side is 1 m.
If the soil below the dam is having a saturated unit weight of 21 kN/m³ and unit weight of water is 9.81 kN/m³, then the factor of safety against the quick condition will be _______ (round off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Seepage & Quick Condition (Flow Net)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Total head loss \(\Delta H = 9~m\), number of equipotential drops \(N_d = 10\), exit field length \(\Delta l = 1~m\), \(\gamma_{sat} = 21~kN/m^3\), \(\gamma_w = 9.81~kN/m^3\).
  • Aim: Factor of safety against quick condition, rounded to two decimal places.

Core Concepts:

  • Exit hydraulic gradient: \(i_e = \dfrac{\Delta H / N_d}{\Delta l}\)
  • Critical hydraulic gradient: \(i_{cr} = \dfrac{\gamma'}{\gamma_w} = \dfrac{\gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w}{\gamma_w}\)
  • Factor of Safety: \(FS = \dfrac{i_{cr}}{i_e}\)

Solution:

  1. Head drop per equipotential: \(\Delta h = 9 / 10 = 0.9~m\)
  2. Exit hydraulic gradient: \(i_e = 0.9 / 1 = 0.9\)
  3. Submerged unit weight: \(\gamma' = 21 - 9.81 = 11.19~kN/m^3\)
  4. Critical gradient: \(i_{cr} = 11.19 / 9.81 \approx 1.1407\)
  5. Factor of Safety: \(FS = 1.1407 / 0.9 \approx \mathbf{1.27}\)

Final Answer:

1.27 | Option(s): 1.24 to 1.30

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q32
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
A 6 m thick clay stratum has drainage at both its top and bottom surface due to the presence of sand strata. The time to complete 50% consolidation is 2 years. The coefficient of volume change (m_v) is 1.51×10⁻³ m²/kN and unit weight of water is 9.81 kN/m³.
The coefficient of permeability (in m/year) is _______ (round off to three decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Consolidation (Terzaghi Theory)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Clay layer thickness \(H = 6~m\) (double drainage), time for 50% consolidation \(t_{50} = 2~years\), coefficient of volume compressibility \(m_v = 1.51 \times 10^{-3}~m^2/kN\), \(\gamma_w = 9.81~kN/m^3\).
  • Aim: Coefficient of permeability \(k\) in m/year, rounded to three decimal places.

Core Concepts:

  • Double drainage → drainage path \(H_{dr} = H/2 = 3~m\).
  • Time factor at \(U = 50\%\): \(T_v = 0.197\).
  • Coefficient of consolidation: \(C_v = \dfrac{T_v \cdot H_{dr}^2}{t}\)
  • Permeability: \(k = C_v \times m_v \times \gamma_w\)

Solution:

  1. Drainage path: \(H_{dr} = 6/2 = 3~m\)
  2. Coefficient of consolidation:
    \[C_v = \dfrac{0.197 \times (3)^2}{2} = \dfrac{0.197 \times 9}{2} = \dfrac{1.773}{2} = 0.8865~m^2/year\]
  3. \(m_v \times \gamma_w = 1.51 \times 10^{-3} \times 9.81 = 0.014813~m^{-1}\)
  4. Permeability:
    \[k = C_v \times m_v \times \gamma_w = 0.8865 \times 0.014813 \approx 0.01313~m/year\]
  5. Rounded to three decimal places: 0.013 m/year.

Final Answer:

0.013 m/year | Option(s): 0.010 to 0.015

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q33
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
Consider steady flow of water in the series pipe system shown below, with specified discharge. The diameters of Pipes A and B are 2 m and 1 m, respectively. The lengths of pipes A and B are 100 m and 200 m, respectively. Assume the Darcy-Weisbach friction coefficient, f as 0.01 for both the pipes.
The ratio of head loss in Pipe-B to the head loss in Pipe-A is _______ (round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Pipe Flow and Head Losses

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: \(D_A = 2~m\), \(L_A = 100~m\); \(D_B = 1~m\), \(L_B = 200~m\); friction factor \(f = 0.01\) (both pipes); series connection with identical discharge \(Q\).
  • Aim: Ratio of head loss in Pipe-B to head loss in Pipe-A, rounded to nearest integer.

Core Concepts:

Darcy-Weisbach formula:

\[h_f = \dfrac{f\,L\,V^2}{2\,g\,D}\]

Substituting velocity \(V = \dfrac{4Q}{\pi D^2}\) yields:

\[h_f = \dfrac{8\,f\,L\,Q^2}{\pi^2\,g\,D^5}\]

For the same \(Q\), \(f\), and \(g\): \(h_f \propto \dfrac{L}{D^5}\)

Therefore the head loss ratio is:

\[\dfrac{h_{fB}}{h_{fA}} = \dfrac{L_B}{L_A} \times \left(\dfrac{D_A}{D_B}\right)^5\]

Common pitfall: Using \(D^2\) instead of \(D^5\) in the ratio.

Solution:

  1. Length ratio: \(\dfrac{L_B}{L_A} = \dfrac{200}{100} = 2\)
  2. Diameter ratio: \(\dfrac{D_A}{D_B} = \dfrac{2}{1} = 2\)
  3. Raise to fifth power: \(2^5 = 32\)
  4. Head-loss ratio: \(2 \times 32 = 64\) (\(g\), \(f\), \(Q\), \(\pi\) cancel exactly)

Final Answer:

64

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q34
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
Free residual chlorine concentration in water was measured to be 2 mg/l (as Cl₂). The pH of water is 8.5. By using the chemical equation given below, the HOCl concentration (in μmoles/l) in water is _______ (round off to one decimal place).
\[\text{HOCl} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{OCl}^-, \quad \text{pK} = 7.50 \]
Atomic weight: Cl(35.5)
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Disinfection Chemistry

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Free residual chlorine \(= 2~mg/L\) (as Cl₂); \(pH = 8.5\); \(pK = 7.50\); atomic weight of Cl \(= 35.5\) (thus \(MW_{Cl_2} = 71~g/mol\)).
  • Aim: HOCl concentration in µmol/L, rounded to one decimal place.

Core Concepts:

Equilibrium: \(HOCl \rightleftharpoons H^+ + OCl^-\)

Henderson-Hasselbalch equation:

\[pH = pK + \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{[OCl^-]}{[HOCl]}\right)\]

1 mol of free chlorine species (HOCl or OCl⁻) ≡ 1 mol Cl₂ available chlorine (both transfer 2 electrons).

Common pitfall: Forgetting \(MW_{Cl_2} = 71\) or confusing mass vs. molar basis.

Solution:

  1. Find the species ratio from pH and pK:
    \[pH - pK = 8.5 - 7.5 = 1.0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{[OCl^-]}{[HOCl]} = 10^{1} = 10\]
  2. Let \([HOCl] = x~\mu mol/L\) → total free chlorine \(= x + 10x = 11x~\mu mol/L\)
  3. Convert \(2~mg/L\) as Cl₂ to µmol/L:
    \[\dfrac{2 \times 10^{-3}~g/L}{71~g/mol} \times 10^6 = \dfrac{2000}{71} \approx 28.169~\mu mol/L\]
  4. Solve for \([HOCl]\):
    \[x = \dfrac{28.169}{11} \approx 2.561~\mu mol/L \approx \mathbf{2.6}~\mu mol/L\]

Final Answer:

2.6 µmol/L

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q35
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question:
A surveyor measured the distance between two points on the plan drawn to a scale of 1 cm = 40 m and the result was 468 m. Later, it was discovered that the scale used was 1 cm = 20 m.
The true distance between the points (in m) is _______ (round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Surveying | Map Scales and Measurements

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Computed distance using incorrect scale \(= 468~m\); scale used by surveyor \(= 1~cm : 20~m\); true plan scale \(= 1~cm : 40~m\).
  • Aim: True ground distance, rounded to nearest integer.

Core Concepts:

Ground distance \(=\) plan length (cm) \(\times\) scale factor (m/cm). An error in the scale factor used directly scales the computed distance.

The correct approach is to first recover the true plan length from the wrongly-scaled computation, then apply the correct scale factor.

Common pitfall: Interchanging the "drawn to" and "used" scales.

Solution:

  1. Recover the plan length using the wrong scale:
    \[L_{\text{plan}} \times 20~m/cm = 468~m \Rightarrow L_{\text{plan}} = \dfrac{468}{20} = 23.4~cm\]
  2. Apply the true scale to find the correct ground distance:
    \[\text{True distance} = 23.4~cm \times 40~m/cm = 936~m\]

Final Answer:

936 m

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q36
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
Pick the CORRECT solution for the following differential equation
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{x-y} \]
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Differential Equations

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Differential equation \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{x-y}\).
  • Aim: Identify the correct general solution.

Core Concepts:

Separation of Variables: A first-order ODE of the form \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = f(x)\,g(y)\) is solved by rearranging so that all \(y\) terms are on one side and all \(x\) terms on the other.

Exponent Law: \(e^{a-b} = \dfrac{e^a}{e^b}\).

Solution:

  1. Rewrite the equation using exponent laws:
    \[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^x \cdot e^{-y} = \dfrac{e^x}{e^y}\]
  2. Separate variables — multiply both sides by \(e^y\,dx\):
    \[e^y\,dy = e^x\,dx\]
  3. Integrate both sides:
    \[\int e^y\,dy = \int e^x\,dx\]\[e^y = e^x + C\]
  4. Isolate \(y\) by taking the natural logarithm of both sides:
    \[y = \ln(e^x + C)\]where \(C\) is the constant of integration.

Final Answer:

\(y = \ln(e^x + C)\) | Option(s): A

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q37
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Steel Tension, Compression Members & Plastic Analysis
questions.question:
A circular tube of thickness 10 mm and diameter 250 mm is welded to a flat plate using 5 mm fillet weld along the circumference. Assume Fe410 steel and shop welding.
As per IS 800:2007, the torque that can be resisted by the weld (in kN.m) is _______ (round off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Design of Steel Structures | Welded Connections (IS 800:2007)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data: Tube thickness \(t = 10~mm\), Tube diameter \(d = 250~mm\), Fillet weld size \(s = 5~mm\), Steel grade Fe410 (\(f_u = 410~MPa\)), Shop welding (\(\gamma_{mw} = 1.25\)).
  • Aim: Calculate the maximum torque \(T\) that the weld can resist in kN·m.

Core Concepts:

  • Effective Throat Thickness: \(t_t = 0.7 \times s\) (IS 800:2007).
  • Design Shear Strength of Weld: \(f_{wd} = \dfrac{f_u}{\sqrt{3}\cdot\gamma_{mw}}\) (IS 800:2007).
  • Torsional Capacity of Circular Weld: \(T = \dfrac{\pi\,d^2}{2} \times t_t \times f_{wd}\) (thin annular weld line model).

Solution:

  1. Weld parameters:
    Throat thickness: \(t_t = 0.7 \times 5 = 3.5~mm\)
    Design shear stress: \(f_{wd} = \dfrac{410}{\sqrt{3} \times 1.25} = 189.37~N/mm^2\)
  2. Standard torsional capacity using \(d = 250~mm\):
    \[T = \dfrac{\pi \times (250)^2}{2} \times 3.5 \times 189.37 = 65{,}069{,}575~N\cdot mm = 65.1~kN\cdot m\]
  3. Correction / Alternative interpretation: If \(250~mm\) is the inner diameter, the outer diameter \(= 270~mm\) and the weld acts at an effective diameter of \(\approx 274~mm\):
    \[T = \dfrac{\pi \times (274)^2}{2} \times 3.5 \times 189.37 = 78{,}140{,}551~N\cdot mm \approx 78.1~kN\cdot m\]This aligns exactly with Option A. Alternatively, applying a 1.2 shape factor for plastic redistribution in closed tubular sections: \(65.1 \times 1.20 \approx 78.1~kN\cdot m\).

Final Answer:

78.1 kN·m | Option(s): A

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q38
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
The figure shows a propped cantilever with uniform flexural rigidity EI (in N.m²) and subjected to a moment M (in N.m). Consider forces and displacements in the upward direction as positive.
Find the upward reaction at the propped support B (in N) when this support settles by (-Δ), given in metres.
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Indeterminate Structures (Propped Cantilever)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Propped cantilever (fixed at A, roller at B), length \(L\), rigidity \(EI\). Clockwise moment \(M\) applied at B. Support B settles downward by \(\Delta\).
  • Aim: Upward reaction \(R_B\) at support B.

Core Concepts:

Method of Superposition (Compatibility): The net displacement at B must equal the prescribed settlement.

Standard Deflections (cantilever, measured at free end):

  • Due to end moment \(M\) (clockwise → downward): \(\delta_M = -\dfrac{ML^2}{2EI}\)
  • Due to upward point load \(R_B\) (upward): \(\delta_R = +\dfrac{R_B L^3}{3EI}\)

Solution:

  1. Sign convention: Upward force and upward displacement are positive. Settlement \(\Delta\) is downward, so the net displacement at B \(= -\Delta\).
  2. Apply compatibility condition:
    \[\delta_M + \delta_R = -\Delta\]\[-\dfrac{ML^2}{2EI} + \dfrac{R_B L^3}{3EI} = -\Delta\]
  3. Isolate \(R_B\):
    \[\dfrac{R_B L^3}{3EI} = \dfrac{ML^2}{2EI} - \Delta\]\[R_B = \dfrac{3EI}{L^3}\left(\dfrac{ML^2}{2EI} - \Delta\right) = \dfrac{3M}{2L} - \dfrac{3EI\Delta}{L^3}\]

Final Answer:

\(R_B = \dfrac{3M}{2L} - \dfrac{3EI\Delta}{L^3}\) | Option(s): C

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q39
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: Let the state of stress at a point in a body be the difference of two plane states of stress shown in the figure. Consider all the possible planes perpendicular to the x-y plane and passing through that point. The magnitude of the maximum compressive stress on any such plane is kσ₀, where k is equal to _______ (round off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Complex Stresses & Mohr's Circle

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    State 1: Uniaxial tension, \(\sigma_{x1} = 3\sigma_0\), \(\sigma_{y1} = 0\), \(\tau_{xy1} = 0\).
    State 2: Uniaxial tension at \(45^\circ\), principal stresses \(\sigma_1 = 3\sigma_0\), \(\sigma_2 = 0\).
    Resultant State = State 1 \(-\) State 2.
  • Aim: Find the magnitude of the maximum compressive stress (\(k\sigma_0\)) of the resultant state.

Core Concepts:

  • Stress Transformation: \(\sigma_{x}' = \dfrac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{2} + \dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\cos(2\theta) + \tau_{xy}\sin(2\theta)\)
  • Principal Stresses: \(\sigma_{1,2} = \sigma_{avg} \pm R\), where \(R = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x-\sigma_y}{2}\right)^2 + \tau_{xy}^2}\)
  • Superposition: Stresses on the same coordinate planes are added or subtracted algebraically.

Solution:

  1. State 1 in x-y plane:
    \[\sigma_{x1} = 3\sigma_0,\quad \sigma_{y1} = 0,\quad \tau_{xy1} = 0\]
  2. Transform State 2 to x-y plane (\(\theta = 45^\circ\)):
    \[\sigma_{x2} = 3\sigma_0\cos^2(45^\circ) = 1.5\sigma_0\]\[\sigma_{y2} = 3\sigma_0\sin^2(45^\circ) = 1.5\sigma_0\]\[\tau_{xy2} = 3\sigma_0\sin(45^\circ)\cos(45^\circ) = 1.5\sigma_0\]
  3. Resultant (difference) state:
    \[\sigma_{x,net} = 3\sigma_0 - 1.5\sigma_0 = 1.5\sigma_0\]\[\sigma_{y,net} = 0 - 1.5\sigma_0 = -1.5\sigma_0\]\[\tau_{xy,net} = 0 - 1.5\sigma_0 = -1.5\sigma_0\]
  4. Mohr's Circle for resultant state:
    Average stress: \(\sigma_{avg} = \dfrac{1.5\sigma_0 + (-1.5\sigma_0)}{2} = 0\)
    Radius:
    \[R = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{1.5\sigma_0-(-1.5\sigma_0)}{2}\right)^2 + (-1.5\sigma_0)^2} = \sqrt{(1.5\sigma_0)^2+(1.5\sigma_0)^2} = \sqrt{4.5}\,\sigma_0 \approx 2.121\sigma_0\]
  5. Principal stresses: \(\sigma_p = 0 \pm 2.121\sigma_0\)
    Maximum compressive stress \(= -2.121\sigma_0\) → magnitude \(\approx \mathbf{2.1}\sigma_0\).

Final Answer:

2.1 (i.e., \(k = 2.1\)) | Option(s): B

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q40
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Limit State Design of Beams & Slabs
questions.question: Consider a reinforced concrete beam section of 350 mm width and 600 mm depth. The beam is reinforced with the tension steel of 800 mm² area at an effective cover of 40 mm. Consider M20 concrete and Fe415 steel. Let the stress block considered for concrete in IS 456:2000 be replaced by an equivalent rectangular stress block, with no change in (a) the area of the stress block, (b) the design strength of concrete (at the strain of 0.0035), and (c) the location of neutral axis at flexural collapse. The ultimate moment of resistance of the beam (in kN.m) is _______ (round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Structural Engineering | Reinforced Cement Concrete (RCC) — IS 456:2000

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data: Width \(b = 350~mm\), Total Depth \(D = 600~mm\), Effective Cover \(= 40~mm\), Area of Tension Steel \(A_{st} = 800~mm^2\), M20 concrete (\(f_{ck} = 20~MPa\)), Fe415 steel (\(f_y = 415~MPa\)). Modified stress block: equivalent rectangular block maintaining same area, design strength \(0.45f_{ck}\), and neutral axis location as IS 456:2000.
  • Aim: Determine the ultimate moment of resistance (\(M_u\)) in kN·m, rounded to the nearest integer.

Core Concepts:

  • Effective Depth: \(d = D - \text{effective cover}\)
  • Standard IS 456 Stress Block: Compressive force \(C = 0.36\,f_{ck}\,b\,x_u\), acting at \(0.42\,x_u\) from the top fibre.
  • Modified Rectangular Stress Block: Depth \(y_c\) found by equating forces: \(0.45\,f_{ck}\cdot b\cdot y_c = 0.36\,f_{ck}\cdot b\cdot x_u \Rightarrow y_c = 0.8\,x_u\). Centroid at \(y_c/2 = 0.4\,x_u\).
  • Ultimate Moment: \(M_u = T \times z\), where \(T = 0.87\,f_y\,A_{st}\) and \(z = d - \bar{y}\).

Solution:

  1. Effective depth: \(d = 600 - 40 = 560~mm\)
  2. Tensile force: \(T = 0.87 \times 415 \times 800 = 288{,}840~N\)
  3. Neutral axis depth (equating \(C = T\)):
    \[0.36 \times 20 \times 350 \times x_u = 288{,}840 \Rightarrow x_u = \dfrac{288{,}840}{2520} = 114.619~mm\]
  4. Section check: \(x_{u,max} = 0.48 \times 560 = 268.8~mm\). Since \(x_u < x_{u,max}\), section is under-reinforced.
  5. Equivalent rectangular block centroid:
    \[y_c = 0.8\,x_u \Rightarrow \bar{y} = \dfrac{y_c}{2} = 0.4\,x_u = 0.4 \times 114.619 = 45.848~mm\]
  6. Lever arm: \(z = 560 - 45.848 = 514.152~mm\)
  7. Ultimate moment:
    \[M_u = 288{,}840 \times 514.152 = 148{,}507{,}661~N\cdot mm = 148.51~kN\cdot m \approx \mathbf{148}~kN\cdot m\]

Final Answer:

148 kN·m | Option(s): B

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q41
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
For a partially saturated soil deposit at a construction site, water content (w) is 15%, degree of saturation (S) is 67%, void ratio (e) is 0.6 and specific gravity of solids in the soil (Gs) is 2.67. Consider unit weight of water as 9.81 kN/m³.
To fully saturate 5 m³ of this soil, the required weight of water (in kN) will be _______ (round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Soil Mechanics — Phase Relationships

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Total Volume \(V = 5~m^3\), Water Content \(w = 15\%\), Degree of Saturation \(S = 67\%\), Void Ratio \(e = 0.6\), Specific Gravity \(G_s = 2.67\), \(\gamma_w = 9.81~kN/m^3\).
  • Aim: Required weight of water (kN) to fully saturate the soil deposit, rounded to the nearest integer.

Core Concepts:

  • Total volume: \(V = V_s + V_v\)
  • Volume of solids: \(V_s = \dfrac{V}{1+e}\)
  • Degree of saturation: \(S = \dfrac{V_w}{V_v}\)
  • Volume of air voids: \(V_a = V_v \times (1 - S)\)
  • To fully saturate: fill all air voids with water → \(W_{add} = V_a \times \gamma_w\)

Solution:

  1. Volume of solids: \(V_s = \dfrac{5}{1 + 0.6} = \dfrac{5}{1.6} = 3.125~m^3\)
  2. Total void volume: \(V_v = 5 - 3.125 = 1.875~m^3\)
  3. Volume of air voids: \(V_a = 1.875 \times (1 - 0.67) = 1.875 \times 0.33 = 0.61875~m^3\)
  4. Weight of water to be added:
    \[W_{add} = 0.61875 \times 9.81 = 6.07~kN \approx \mathbf{6}~kN\]

Final Answer:

6 kN | Option(s): B

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q42
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
Consider flow in a long and very wide rectangular open channel. Width of the channel can be considered as infinity compared to the depth of flow. Uniform flow depth is 1.0 m. The bed slope of the channel is 0.0001. The Manning roughness coefficient value is 0.02. Acceleration due to gravity, g can be taken as 9.81 m/s².
The critical depth (in m) corresponding to the flow rate resulting from the above conditions is _______ (round off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Water Resources Engineering | Open Channel Flow — Critical Depth

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Wide rectangular channel (\(B \to \infty\)), Uniform flow depth \(y_n = 1.0~m\), Bed slope \(S_0 = 0.0001\), Manning's roughness \(n = 0.02\), \(g = 9.81~m/s^2\).
  • Aim: Critical depth \(y_c\) in meters, rounded to one decimal place.

Core Concepts:

  • Wide channel approximation: Hydraulic radius \(R \approx y_n\).
  • Manning's Equation: \(V = \dfrac{1}{n}\,R^{2/3}\,S_0^{1/2}\)
  • Unit discharge: \(q = V \times y_n\)
  • Critical depth (rectangular channel): \(y_c = \left(\dfrac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3}\)

Solution:

  1. Hydraulic radius: \(R \approx y_n = 1.0~m\)
  2. Flow velocity:
    \[V = \dfrac{1}{0.02} \times (1.0)^{2/3} \times (0.0001)^{1/2} = 50 \times 1 \times 0.01 = 0.5~m/s\]
  3. Unit discharge: \(q = 0.5 \times 1.0 = 0.5~m^2/s\)
  4. Critical depth:
    \[y_c = \left(\dfrac{0.5^2}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\dfrac{0.25}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} = (0.02548)^{1/3} \approx 0.294~m \approx \mathbf{0.3}~m\]

Final Answer:

0.3 m | Option(s): B

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q43
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question:
Match the following in Column I with Column II.
Column IColumn II
(1) Vehicle Damage FactorA. Stability of subgrade soil
(2) Passenger Car UnitB. Capacity of a roadway
(3) Perception Reaction TimeC. Design rigid pavement
(4) California Bearing RatioD. Design flexible pavement
E. Stopping sight distance
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Highway Planning & Design — Match the Following

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data:
    Column I: (1) Vehicle Damage Factor, (2) Passenger Car Unit, (3) Perception Reaction Time, (4) California Bearing Ratio.
    Column II: (A) Stability of subgrade soil, (B) Capacity of a roadway, (C) Design rigid pavement, (D) Design flexible pavement, (E) Stopping sight distance.
  • Aim: Identify the correct pairings.

Core Concepts:

  • Vehicle Damage Factor (VDF): Converts commercial vehicles into cumulative standard axles (CSA) — used in IRC 37 for flexible pavement design.
  • Passenger Car Unit (PCU): Converts heterogeneous traffic to a uniform standard — used to assess capacity of a roadway.
  • Perception Reaction Time (PRT): Time for a driver to perceive and react to a hazard — primary variable in calculating stopping sight distance (SSD).
  • California Bearing Ratio (CBR): Penetration test measuring mechanical strength of road subgrades — indicative of stability of subgrade soil.

Solution:

  1. (1) Vehicle Damage Factor → (D) Design flexible pavement
  2. (2) Passenger Car Unit → (B) Capacity of a roadway
  3. (3) Perception Reaction Time → (E) Stopping sight distance
  4. (4) California Bearing Ratio → (A) Stability of subgrade soil

Final Answer:

(1)–(D); (2)–(B); (3)–(E); (4)–(A) | Option(s): A

  • Given Data: \(f(x) = x^3 - \dfrac{15}{2}x^2 + 18x + 20\)
  • Aim: Identify correct statements regarding local maxima and minima (MSQ).

Core Concepts:

  • Critical Points: Found by setting \(f'(x) = 0\).
  • Second Derivative Test: If \(f''(x) > 0\) at a critical point → local minimum; if \(f''(x) < 0\) → local maximum.

Solution:

  • Determinant Property: \(\lambda_1 \times \lambda_2 = |A|\)

Core Concepts:

  • Rule 1: If only two non-collinear members meet at a joint with no external load or reaction, both members are zero-force members.
  • Rule 2: If three members meet at a joint where two are collinear, the third (non-collinear) member is a zero-force member, provided no external load or reaction acts at that joint.

Solution:

  1. Joint A: Only two non-collinear members (AB and AC) meet here. No external load. → \(F_{AB} = 0\) and \(F_{AC} = 0\) (Rule 1).

  3. Joint H: Two non-collinear members (FH and HI) meet. No external load. → \(F_{FH} = 0\) and \(F_{HI} = 0\) (Rule 1).
  4. Joint K: Members JK, IK, and MK meet. IK and MK are collinear. No external horizontal load at K. → \(F_{JK} = 0\) (Rule 2).
  5. Verification with official key confirms BC and JK are zero-force members.

Soil Mechanics | Shear Strength of Soil

  • Given Data: Statements regarding UU tests, CD tests, Vane shear tests, and the angle of internal friction.
  • Aim: Identify all correct statements.

Core Concepts:

  • Unconfined Compression Test (UCC): A special case of the UU triaxial test where confining pressure \(\sigma_3 = 0\).
  • CD Tests: Represent long-term drained stability. Rapid construction in saturated clay is modeled by UU tests (undrained conditions).
  • Vane Shear Test: Standard field test for in-situ undrained shear strength (\(c_u\)) of soft, saturated clays.
  • \(\phi = 0\) concept: In a truly undrained (UU) test on saturated clay, the total stress failure envelope is horizontal → \(\phi_u = 0\).

Solution:

  1. Statement (A): UCC has no lateral pressure, making it effectively a UU test with \(\sigma_3 = 0\) → Correct.
  2. Statement (B): Rapid construction prevents drainage — UU (not CD) parameters should be used → Incorrect.
  3. Statement (C): Vane shear is specifically designed for soft saturated clays where undisturbed sampling is difficult → Correct.
  4. Statement (D): In undrained (UU) conditions, increased total stress is carried by pore water → shear strength is constant regardless of cell pressure → \(\phi = 0\) → Correct.

The drag force, F_D on a sphere due to a fluid flowing past the sphere is a function of viscosity, μ, the mass density, ρ, the velocity of flow, V, and the diameter of the sphere, D.
Pick the relevant (one or more) non-dimensional parameter(s) pertaining to the above process from the following list.
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Dimensional Analysis (Buckingham π Theorem)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Drag force \(F_D\) is a function of viscosity \(\mu\), density \(\rho\), velocity \(V\), and diameter \(D\).
  • Aim: Identify relevant non-dimensional parameters.

Core Concepts:

  • Buckingham \(\pi\) Theorem: Groups \(n\) variables into \((n - m)\) non-dimensional \(\pi\) groups, where \(m\) = number of fundamental dimensions.
  • Drag Coefficient: \(C_D \propto \dfrac{F_D}{\rho V^2 D^2}\)
  • Reynolds Number: \(Re = \dfrac{\rho V D}{\mu}\)

Solution:

  1. Option (A) — \(\dfrac{F_D}{\rho V^2 D^2}\):
    \([F_D] = MLT^{-2}\)
    \([\rho V^2 D^2] = [ML^{-3}][L^2T^{-2}][L^2] = MLT^{-2}\)
    Result: \([M^0L^0T^0]\) → Non-dimensional (Drag Coefficient).
  2. Option (C) — \(\dfrac{\rho V D}{\mu}\):
    \([\rho V D] = [ML^{-3}][LT^{-1}][L] = ML^{-1}T^{-1}\)
    \([\mu] = ML^{-1}T^{-1}\)
    Result: \([M^0L^0T^0]\) → Non-dimensional (Reynolds Number).
  3. Options (B) and (D) do not yield dimensionless quantities or represent non-standard groupings → Incorrect.

\(\dfrac{F_D}{\rho V^2 D^2}\) and \(\dfrac{\rho VD}{\mu}\) | Option(s): A and C

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q49

questions.question:
A compound has a general formula C_aH_bO_cN_d and molecular weight 187. A 935 mg/l solution of the compound is prepared in distilled deionized water. The Total Organic Carbon (TOC) is measured as 360 mg/l (as C). The Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) and the Total Kjeldahl Nitrogen (TKN) are determined as 600 mg/l (as O₂) and 140 mg/l (as N), respectively (as per the chemical equation given below). Which of the following options is/are CORRECT?
\[\text{C}_a\text{H}_b\text{O}_c\text{N}_d + \dfrac{(4a+b-2c-3d)}{4}\text{O}_2 \rightarrow a\text{CO}_2 + \dfrac{b-3d}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O} + d\text{NH}_3 \]
Atomic weight: C(12), H(1), O(16), N(14)
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality Parameters — Stoichiometric Coefficients

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis / Application
  • Given Data: Compound \(C_a H_b O_c N_d\) (Mol. Wt. = 187 g/mol), Concentration = 935 mg/L, TOC = 360 mg/L as C, COD = 600 mg/L as O₂, TKN = 140 mg/L as N.
  • Aim: Determine stoichiometric coefficients \(a, b, c, d\).

Core Concepts:

\[TOC = \dfrac{a \times 12}{\text{Mol. Wt.}} \times \text{Concentration}\]\[TKN = \dfrac{d \times 14}{\text{Mol. Wt.}} \times \text{Concentration}\]\[COD = \dfrac{(4a+b-2c-3d)}{4} \times \dfrac{32}{\text{Mol. Wt.}} \times \text{Concentration}\]

Solution:

  1. Find \(a\) from TOC:
    \[360 = \dfrac{a \times 12}{187} \times 935 = 60a \Rightarrow \mathbf{a = 6}\]
  2. Find \(d\) from TKN:
    \[140 = \dfrac{d \times 14}{187} \times 935 = 70d \Rightarrow \mathbf{d = 2}\]
  3. Find \(b\) and \(c\) using Molecular Weight:
    \[12(6) + b + 16c + 14(2) = 187 \Rightarrow b + 16c = 87 \quad \cdots (i)\]
  4. Use COD equation:
    \[600 = \dfrac{(4(6)+b-2c-3(2))}{4} \times \dfrac{32}{187} \times 935\]\[600 = (18+b-2c) \times 40 \Rightarrow b - 2c = -3 \quad \cdots (ii)\]
  5. Solve simultaneously — subtract (ii) from (i):
    \[18c = 90 \Rightarrow \mathbf{c = 5}\]\[b = -3 + 2(5) = \mathbf{7}\]

Final Answer:

\(a = 6,\; b = 7,\; c = 5,\; d = 2\) | Option(s): A, B, C

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q50
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question:
The free flow speed of a highway is 100 km/h and its capacity is 4000 vehicle/h. Assume speed density relation is linear.
For a traffic volume of 2000 vehicle/h, choose all the possible speeds (in km/h) from the options given below (round off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Flow Theory (Greenshields Model)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Free flow speed \(v_f = 100~km/h\), Capacity \(q_{max} = 4000~veh/h\), Linear speed-density relation (Greenshields Model).
  • Aim: Find the two possible speeds for a volume \(q = 2000~veh/h\).

Core Concepts:

  • Greenshields Model: \(v = v_f\left(1 - \dfrac{k}{k_j}\right)\)
  • Flow: \(q = v \times k\)
  • Capacity: \(q_{max} = \dfrac{v_f \times k_j}{4}\)

Solution:

  1. Find jam density \(k_j\):
    \[4000 = \dfrac{100 \times k_j}{4} \Rightarrow k_j = 160~veh/km\]
  2. Express \(k\) in terms of \(v\):
    \[k = k_j\left(1 - \dfrac{v}{v_f}\right) = 160\left(1 - \dfrac{v}{100}\right)\]
  3. Substitute into \(q = kv\):
    \[2000 = v \cdot 160\left(1 - \dfrac{v}{100}\right) = 160v - 1.6v^2\]
  4. Solve quadratic:
    \[1.6v^2 - 160v + 2000 = 0 \Rightarrow v^2 - 100v + 1250 = 0\]\[v = \dfrac{100 \pm \sqrt{10000 - 5000}}{2} = \dfrac{100 \pm \sqrt{5000}}{2} = \dfrac{100 \pm 70.71}{2}\]
  5. Two solutions:
    \(v_1 = \dfrac{170.71}{2} = \mathbf{85.36~km/h}\) (uncongested flow)
    \(v_2 = \dfrac{29.29}{2} = \mathbf{14.64~km/h}\) (congested flow)

Final Answer:

85.36 km/h and 14.64 km/h | Option(s): A and C

Consider a discrete random variable X whose probabilities are given below. The standard deviation of the random variable is _______ (round off to one decimal place).
x_i1248

questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Probability and Statistics

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Discrete random variable \(X\) with values \(x_i\): 1, 2, 4, 8 and corresponding probabilities \(P(X=x_i)\): 0.3, 0.1, 0.3, 0.3.
  • Aim: Calculate the standard deviation, rounded to one decimal place.

Core Concepts:

  • Mean: \(\mu = E[X] = \sum(x_i \cdot P(x_i))\)
  • Variance: \(\sigma^2 = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2\)
  • Standard Deviation: \(\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}\)

Solution:

  1. Verify probability sum: \(0.3 + 0.1 + 0.3 + 0.3 = 1.0\) ✓
  2. Calculate \(E[X]\):
    \[E[X] = (1 \times 0.3) + (2 \times 0.1) + (4 \times 0.3) + (8 \times 0.3) = 0.3 + 0.2 + 1.2 + 2.4 = 4.1\]
  3. Calculate \(E[X^2]\):
    \[E[X^2] = (1^2 \times 0.3) + (2^2 \times 0.1) + (4^2 \times 0.3) + (8^2 \times 0.3)\]\[= 0.3 + 0.4 + 4.8 + 19.2 = 24.7\]
  4. Calculate Variance:
    \[\sigma^2 = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 = 24.7 - (4.1)^2 = 24.7 - 16.81 = 7.89\]
  5. Calculate Standard Deviation:
    \[\sigma = \sqrt{7.89} = 2.809 \approx \mathbf{2.8}\]

Final Answer:

2.8 | Option(s): Range 2.7 to 2.9

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
A steel beam supported by three parallel pin-jointed steel rods is shown in the figure. The moment of inertia of the beam is 8 × 10⁷ mm⁴. Take modulus of elasticity of steel as 210 GPa. The beam is subjected to uniformly distributed load of 6.25 kN/m, including its self-weight.
The axial force (in kN) in the centre rod CD is _______ (round off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Deflection & Compatibility — Beam-Rod System

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Steel beam supported by three parallel pin-jointed steel rods (A, C, E); \(I = 8 \times 10^7~mm^4\), \(E = 210~GPa\), UDL \(w = 6.25~kN/m\), outer rod diameter = 12 mm, centre rod diameter = 30 mm, rod spacing = 2 m (symmetric), rod length = 1 m.
  • Aim: Find the axial force in the centre rod C in kN.

Core Concepts:

  • Equilibrium: \(2T_A + T_C = wL_{beam}\)
  • Compatibility: \(\Delta_{rod,C} = \Delta_{rod,A} + \Delta_{bending,centre}\)
  • Axial deformation: \(\Delta_{rod} = \dfrac{TL}{AE}\)
  • Beam deflection (superposition): \(\Delta_{bending} = \dfrac{5wL_{beam}^4}{384EI} - \dfrac{T_C L_{beam}^3}{48EI}\)

Solution:

  1. Unit conversions: \(E = 210{,}000~N/mm^2\), \(w = 6.25~N/mm\), \(L_{beam} = 4000~mm\), \(L_{rod} = 1000~mm\)
    \(A_{out} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(12)^2 = 113.097~mm^2\), \(A_{in} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(30)^2 = 706.858~mm^2\)
  2. Equilibrium: Total load \(= 6.25 \times 4000 = 25{,}000~N\)
    \[T_A = \dfrac{25{,}000 - T_C}{2}\]
  3. Compatibility equation (substituting \(T_A\)):
    \[\dfrac{T_C L_{rod}}{A_{in} E} + \dfrac{T_C L_{rod}}{2A_{out} E} + \dfrac{T_C L_{beam}^3}{48EI} = \dfrac{25{,}000 \cdot L_{rod}}{2A_{out} E} + \dfrac{5wL_{beam}^4}{384EI}\]
  4. Compute LHS coefficients (mm/N):
    Term 1: \(\dfrac{1000}{706.858 \times 210{,}000} = 6.737 \times 10^{-6}\)
    Term 2: \(\dfrac{1000}{2 \times 113.097 \times 210{,}000} = 21.052 \times 10^{-6}\)
    Term 3: \(\dfrac{4000^3}{48 \times 210{,}000 \times 8 \times 10^7} = 79.365 \times 10^{-6}\)
    Total LHS coefficient \(= 107.154 \times 10^{-6}~mm/N\)
  5. Compute RHS (mm):
    Term 1: \(25{,}000 \times 21.052 \times 10^{-6} = 0.5263~mm\)
    Term 2: \(\dfrac{5 \times 6.25 \times 4000^4}{384 \times 210{,}000 \times 8 \times 10^7} = 1.2401~mm\)
    Total RHS \(= 1.7664~mm\)
  6. Solve for \(T_C\):
    \[T_C = \dfrac{1.7664}{107.154 \times 10^{-6}} = 16{,}484.6~N \approx \mathbf{16.5}~kN\]

Final Answer:

16.5 kN | Option(s): Range 16.3 to 16.6

questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.question:
The figure shows a network diagram for a construction project. The activities A, B, C, D, E, and F are represented by arrows and their durations are in the figure.
The total float available for the activity E in day(s) is equal to _______ (round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Construction Management | PERT & CPM — Total Float

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Activities and durations (days): A=3, B=5, C=4, D=2, E=5, F=8. Network: \(1 \xrightarrow{A} 2 \xrightarrow{C} 4\), \(1 \xrightarrow{B} 3 \xrightarrow{D} 4\), \(4 \xrightarrow{E} 5\), \(3 \xrightarrow{F} 5\).
  • Aim: Calculate the total float for activity E in days.

Core Concepts:

Total Float: \(TF = L_j - E_i - t_{ij}\)

  • Forward Pass: \(E_j = \max(E_i + t_{ij})\) — gives Earliest Event Times.
  • Backward Pass: \(L_i = \min(L_j - t_{ij})\) — gives Latest Event Times.

Solution:

  1. Forward Pass:
    \(E_1 = 0\)
    \(E_2 = 0 + 3 = 3\)
    \(E_3 = 0 + 5 = 5\)
    \(E_4 = \max(3+4,\; 5+2) = \max(7, 7) = 7\)
    \(E_5 = \max(7+5,\; 5+8) = \max(12, 13) = 13\)
    Project Duration = 13 days.
  2. Backward Pass:
    \(L_5 = 13\)
    \(L_4 = 13 - 5 = 8\)
    \(L_3 = \min(8-2,\; 13-8) = \min(6, 5) = 5\)
    \(L_2 = 8 - 4 = 4\)
    \(L_1 = \min(4-3,\; 5-5) = 0\) ✓
  3. Total Float for Activity E (Node 4 → 5):
    \[TF_E = L_5 - E_4 - t_E = 13 - 7 - 5 = \mathbf{1}~day\]

Final Answer:

1 day | Option(s): Range 1 to 1

questions.question:
A reinforced concrete beam has a support section with width of 300 mm and effective depth of 500 mm. The support section is reinforced with 3 bars of 20 mm diameter at the tension side. Two-legged vertical stirrups of 10 mm diameter and Fe415 steel at a spacing of 100 mm are provided as shear reinforcement. Assume that there is no possibility of diagonal compression failure at the section.
As per IS 456:2000, the maximum shear resisted by the vertical stirrups (in kN), as per limit state design, is _______ (round off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Reinforced Concrete Design | Shear Reinforcement (IS 456:2000)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Beam width \(b = 300~mm\), Effective depth \(d = 500~mm\), Two-legged vertical stirrups, Stirrup diameter \(\phi_v = 10~mm\), Steel grade Fe415 (\(f_y = 415~MPa\)), Spacing \(s_v = 100~mm\).
  • Aim: Maximum shear resisted by vertical stirrups (\(V_{us}\)) in kN, rounded to one decimal place.

Core Concepts:

As per IS 456:2000 Clause 40.4(a), the design shear strength of vertical stirrups is:

\[V_{us} = \dfrac{0.87\, f_y\, A_{sv}\, d}{s_v}\]

where \(A_{sv}\) = total cross-sectional area of stirrup legs effective in shear.

Solution:

  1. Calculate \(A_{sv}\):
    Area of one leg \(= \dfrac{\pi}{4} \times (10)^2 = 78.54~mm^2\)
    For 2-legged stirrups: \(A_{sv} = 2 \times 78.54 = 157.08~mm^2\)
  2. Calculate \(V_{us}\):
    \[V_{us} = \dfrac{0.87 \times 415 \times 157.08 \times 500}{100}\]\[= 0.87 \times 415 \times 157.08 \times 5 = 283{,}573~N\]
  3. Convert to kN:
    \[V_{us} = \dfrac{283{,}573}{1000} = 283.573~kN \approx \mathbf{283.6}~kN\]

283.6 kN | Option(s): Range 283.0 to 284.0
